quote: Praestabilirte Harmonie zwischen Denken u. Sein [-hat doch-] (Einfachheit der Theorie u. der Experimente, und Uebereinstimmung der Wirklichkeit mit schönen u. einfachen Theorien) hat doch einen tiefere Grund. Diesen finden! Philosophisches Problem!
english: Pre-established harmony between thinking and being (simplicity of theory and of experiments, and agreement of reality with beautiful and simple theories) must have a deeper reason. Find it! Philosophical problem!
topic: Philosophical notes on applying statistical principles to mathematical facts, the sameness of the simplest logical propositions, pre-established harmony between thought and being, intellectual refinement versus thermodynamic degradation, monism, the axiomatic method as the general form of thinking, and the 'proof of all proofs'.

triage.modern_statement: This is not a mathematical research question. It is a philosophical problem: why does nature agree with simple, beautiful mathematical theories? Why does mathematics that was developed for its own sake turn out to describe physics? Today this is called the problem of the 'pre-established harmony' between mathematics and physics, or the 'unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences' (Wigner). It is an open question in the philosophy of science and mathematics and has no formal mathematical statement.
triage.answered_by: No one has given an accepted answer. Hilbert came back to the question in public in his 1930 Königsberg address 'Naturerkennen und Logik' (Naturwissenschaften 18, 959–963). There he used conic sections and Einstein's general relativity as examples of pre-established harmony and suggested that the explanation lies in 'the formal element' shared by nature and the intellect. Wigner later made the problem famous (lecture 1959, published 1960). Historians such as Pyenson (1982) and Kragh (2015) have written about the idea. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem.

evidence.claim: In 'Naturerkennen und Logik' (Naturwissenschaften, 28 Nov 1930, pp. 959–963), Hilbert describes a phenomenon that he calls pre-established harmony, in a different sense from Leibniz. He calls Einstein's relativity theory its grandest example and says the agreement between nature and thought, experiment and theory, can only be understood through the formal element on both sides.

Scan of the published 1930 article. Conic sections were studied long before anyone knew that planets or electrons move on such orbits. General relativity is called the most wonderful example of pre-established harmony.
Springer record of D. Hilbert, 'Naturerkennen und Logik', Naturwissenschaften vol. 18, pp. 959–963, November 1930.
Wigner introduced the phrase 'unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics' in 1960 for the unexpectedly broad and accurate applicability of mathematics to the physical sciences.

Kragh (Science & Education 24, 2015, pp. 515–527) traces how the idea of a pre-established harmony between mathematics and physics has, for more than a century, shaped the rhetoric and research of mathematicians and theoretical physicists.
Wigner's paper continues to attract comment from scientists, applied mathematicians and philosophers.

triage.why: Hilbert himself calls this note a 'philosophical problem', and it has no mathematical content to prove or disprove. The idea is well known: Hilbert discussed it publicly in 1930, giving at most a sketch of an explanation (the formal element common to nature and thought), and Wigner's 1960 paper made it famous. Philosophers and historians still debate it (e.g. Kragh 2015, commentary on Wigner), and there is no agreed answer, so it is a known, open and still active philosophical question rather than a solved problem. The sources do not show whether this diary note directly led to the 1930 address; the link is suggested only by the matching wording.
